claim: The twinning rate has increased dramatically in all developed countries during the last decades due to the sharp rise in medically assisted reproduction and delayed childbearing.
source: Because of the sharp rise in medically assisted reproduction and delayed childbearing during the last decades, the twinning rate has increased dramatically in all developed countries (Pison et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pison et al., 2015

claim: Twin pregnancies are associated with greater health risks for both infants and mothers.
source: This rise in twinning rate represents an important public health issue since twin pregnancies are associated with greater health risks for both infants and mothers (Cheong-See et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cheong-See et al., 2016

claim: Compared to singletons, twin babies are more often subjected to multiple adverse neonatal outcomes, including preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age, and neonatal death.
source: Compared to singletons, twin babies are more often subjected to multiple adverse neonatal outcomes, including preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age, and neonatal death (Cheong-See et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cheong-See et al., 2016

claim: Approximately 16% of twin pregnancies have birth weight discordance of at least 20%.
source: Approximately 16% of twin pregnancies have birth weight discordance of at least 20%, which might also contribute to elevated risk of perinatal and neonatal mortality (Blickstein and Kalish, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Blickstein and Kalish, 2003

claim: Birth weight discordance of at least 20% in twin pregnancies might contribute to elevated risk of perinatal and neonatal mortality.
source: Approximately 16% of twin pregnancies have birth weight discordance of at least 20%, which might also contribute to elevated risk of perinatal and neonatal mortality (Blickstein and Kalish, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Blickstein and Kalish, 2003, with speculative language 'might'

claim: A considerable proportion of twins experience a very early loss of their co-twin.
source: Consequently, a considerable proportion of twins experience a very early loss of their co-twin.
evidence: Inferred from the preceding discussion of twin pregnancy complications and mortality risks

claim: Loss of a co-twin by death in childhood or adulthood is associated with considerable mental morbidities among the surviving twins.
source: Previous studies indicate that loss of a co-twin by death in childhood or adulthood is associated with considerable mental morbidities among the surviving twins (Segal and Bouchard, 1993; Woodward, 1988).
evidence: Supported by citations to Segal and Bouchard, 1993 and Woodward, 1988

claim: Loss of a co-twin beyond age 2 is associated with an increased risk of psychiatric disorders compared to loss of a full (non-twin) sibling.
source: Our recent findings suggest an increased risk of psychiatric disorders after a loss of co-twin, compared to loss of a full (non-twin) sibling, beyond age 2 (Song et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Song et al., 2020

claim: The greater risk increase after loss of a co-twin might be due to the stronger emotional bond between twins.
source: The greater risk increase after loss of a co-twin might be due to the stronger emotional bond between twins (Rosendahl SP and Björklund, 2013; Segal and Ream, 1998) and the greater genetic relatedness, in the case of monozygotic twins (Segal and Ream, 1998; Parkes, 1993; Neyer, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations with speculative language 'might be due to'

claim: The greater risk increase after loss of a co-twin might be due to greater genetic relatedness in the case of monozygotic twins.
source: The greater risk increase after loss of a co-twin might be due to the stronger emotional bond between twins (Rosendahl SP and Björklund, 2013; Segal and Ream, 1998) and the greater genetic relatedness, in the case of monozygotic twins (Segal and Ream, 1998; Parkes, 1993; Neyer, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations with speculative language 'might be due to'

claim: With cognitive immaturity and limited (or no) afterbirth interactions, a co-twin loss at birth leaves little room for a twin bond to be established.
source: In contrast, with cognitive immaturity and limited (or no) afterbirth interactions, a co-twin loss at birth or during the neonatal period leaves little room for a twin bond to be established and therefore it seems implausible that the mental health of the surviving twin would be affected by such a loss.
evidence: Based on logical reasoning about cognitive development and bonding

claim: It seems implausible that the mental health of the surviving twin would be affected by a co-twin loss at birth.
source: In contrast, with cognitive immaturity and limited (or no) afterbirth interactions, a co-twin loss at birth or during the neonatal period leaves little room for a twin bond to be established and therefore it seems implausible that the mental health of the surviving twin would be affected by such a loss.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on cognitive development theory

claim: Several scientific and media accounts describe unexpected lingering sorrow among twins who lost their co-twin at or shortly after birth.
source: However, several scientific and media accounts describe unexpected lingering sorrow among twins who lost their co-twin at or shortly after birth, even among the twins that didn't know they were born as twins (Morgan, 2014; lone twin network, 2020; Woodward, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Morgan, 2014; lone twin network, 2020; Woodward, 2010

claim: Lingering sorrow has been reported even among twins that didn't know they were born as twins.
source: However, several scientific and media accounts describe unexpected lingering sorrow among twins who lost their co-twin at or shortly after birth, even among the twins that didn't know they were born as twins (Morgan, 2014; lone twin network, 2020; Woodward, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Morgan, 2014; lone twin network, 2020; Woodward, 2010

claim: The parenting of bereaved parents after the perinatal loss of one twin baby may leave the surviving twin vulnerable for mental morbidities.
source: It is further possible that the parenting of bereaved parents after the perinatal loss of one twin baby may leave the surviving twin vulnerable for mental morbidities (Lamb, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lamb, 2002 with speculative language 'it is possible'

claim: The study included all Swedish-born twins that lost a co-twin at birth (defined as death within 60 days after birth) between 1973 and 2011 (n = 787).
source: We contrasted rate of first-onset psychiatric disorders among all Swedish-born twins whose co-twin died within 60 days after birth between 1973 and 2011 (n = 787) to that of 3935 matched unexposed twins, 3935 matched singletons (both matched to the exposed twins by birth year, sex, and birth characteristics), and 880 full siblings of the exposed twins.

claim: The study included 3935 matched unexposed twins as a comparison group.
source: We contrasted rate of first-onset psychiatric disorders among all Swedish-born twins whose co-twin died within 60 days after birth between 1973 and 2011 (n = 787) to that of 3935 matched unexposed twins, 3935 matched singletons (both matched to the exposed twins by birth year, sex, and birth characteristics), and 880 full siblings of the exposed twins.

claim: The study included 3935 matched singletons as a comparison group.
source: We contrasted rate of first-onset psychiatric disorders among all Swedish-born twins whose co-twin died within 60 days after birth between 1973 and 2011 (n = 787) to that of 3935 matched unexposed twins, 3935 matched singletons (both matched to the exposed twins by birth year, sex, and birth characteristics), and 880 full siblings of the exposed twins.

claim: The study included 880 full siblings of the exposed twins as a comparison group.
source: We contrasted rate of first-onset psychiatric disorders among all Swedish-born twins whose co-twin died within 60 days after birth between 1973 and 2011 (n = 787) to that of 3935 matched unexposed twins, 3935 matched singletons (both matched to the exposed twins by birth year, sex, and birth characteristics), and 880 full siblings of the exposed twins.

claim: The median follow-up time was 19 years.
source: During a median of 19-year follow-up, exposed twins were at increased risk of first-onset psychiatric disorders (hazard ratio = 1.56, 95%CI 1.30–1.87) compared with unexposed twins.

claim: Exposed twins were at increased risk of first-onset psychiatric disorders (hazard ratio = 1.56, 95%CI 1.30–1.87) compared with unexposed twins.
source: During a median of 19-year follow-up, exposed twins were at increased risk of first-onset psychiatric disorders (hazard ratio = 1.56, 95%CI 1.30–1.87) compared with unexposed twins.
evidence: Primary study finding with statistical analysis

claim: The strongest association was observed for emotional disorders.
source: We observed the strongest association for emotional disorders and for psychiatric disorders diagnosed before the age of 25.

claim: The strongest association was observed for psychiatric disorders diagnosed before the age of 25.
source: We observed the strongest association for emotional disorders and for psychiatric disorders diagnosed before the age of 25.

claim: Comparisons with matched singletons rendered similar results to comparisons with unexposed twins.
source: Comparisons with matched singletons and the twin's full siblings rendered similar results, corroborating an association of loss of a co-twin at birth with subsequent risk of psychiatric disorders.

claim: Comparisons with the twin's full siblings rendered similar results to comparisons with unexposed twins.
source: Comparisons with matched singletons and the twin's full siblings rendered similar results, corroborating an association of loss of a co-twin at birth with subsequent risk of psychiatric disorders.

claim: The results corroborate an association of loss of a co-twin at birth with subsequent risk of psychiatric disorders.
source: Comparisons with matched singletons and the twin's full siblings rendered similar results, corroborating an association of loss of a co-twin at birth with subsequent risk of psychiatric disorders.
evidence: Overall conclusion from multiple comparison analyses

claim: The population-based matched cohort accumulated 169,507 person-years at risk.
source: In total, the population-based matched cohort accumulated 169,507 person-years at risk, with a median of 19 years of follow-up (Table 1).

claim: 54% of the exposed twins were male.
source: The exposed twins had an almost equal sex distribution (54% were male).

claim: There was little difference in birth weight for GA between exposed twins and matched unexposed twins and singletons.
source: While there was little difference in birth weight for GA, maternal educational level, and family history of psychiatric disorders, exposed twins tended to have lower Apgar score, older mothers at childbirth, and higher maternal cohabitation rate than matched unexposed twins and singletons.

claim: There was little difference in maternal educational level between exposed twins and matched unexposed twins and singletons.
source: While there was little difference in birth weight for GA, maternal educational level, and family history of psychiatric disorders, exposed twins tended to have lower Apgar score, older mothers at childbirth, and higher maternal cohabitation rate than matched unexposed twins and singletons.

claim: There was little difference in family history of psychiatric disorders between exposed twins and matched unexposed twins and singletons.
source: While there was little difference in birth weight for GA, maternal educational level, and family history of psychiatric disorders, exposed twins tended to have lower Apgar score, older mothers at childbirth, and higher maternal cohabitation rate than matched unexposed twins and singletons.

claim: Exposed twins tended to have lower Apgar score than matched unexposed twins and singletons.
source: While there was little difference in birth weight for GA, maternal educational level, and family history of psychiatric disorders, exposed twins tended to have lower Apgar score, older mothers at childbirth, and higher maternal cohabitation rate than matched unexposed twins and singletons.

claim: Exposed twins tended to have older mothers at childbirth than matched unexposed twins and singletons.
source: While there was little difference in birth weight for GA, maternal educational level, and family history of psychiatric disorders, exposed twins tended to have lower Apgar score, older mothers at childbirth, and higher maternal cohabitation rate than matched unexposed twins and singletons.

claim: Exposed twins tended to have higher maternal cohabitation rate than matched unexposed twins and singletons.
source: While there was little difference in birth weight for GA, maternal educational level, and family history of psychiatric disorders, exposed twins tended to have lower Apgar score, older mothers at childbirth, and higher maternal cohabitation rate than matched unexposed twins and singletons.

claim: In the twin-sibling family cohort, maternal characteristics were identical or similar between exposed twins and their full siblings.
source: As expected, in the twin-sibling family cohort, maternal characteristics were identical or similar between exposed twins and their full siblings, although birth characteristics (e.g., GA, birth weight for GA, and Apgar score) were different between these two groups (Table 1).
evidence: Comparison of baseline characteristics in sibling cohort

claim: In the twin-sibling family cohort, birth characteristics (e.g., GA, birth weight for GA, and Apgar score) were different between exposed twins and their full siblings.
source: As expected, in the twin-sibling family cohort, maternal characteristics were identical or similar between exposed twins and their full siblings, although birth characteristics (e.g., GA, birth weight for GA, and Apgar score) were different between these two groups (Table 1).
evidence: Comparison of baseline characteristics in sibling cohort

claim: During follow-up, 1501 individuals with incident psychiatric disorders were identified in the population-based matched cohort.
source: During the follow-up, we identified 1501 individuals with incident psychiatric disorders in the population-based matched cohort, including 178 cases among the exposed twins, 600 among the matched unexposed twins, and 723 among the matched singletons, corresponding to a crude incidence rate (IR) of 12.08, 7.76, and 9.33 per 1000 person-years, respectively (Table 2).

claim: 178 cases of psychiatric disorders were identified among the exposed twins.
source: During the follow-up, we identified 1501 individuals with incident psychiatric disorders in the population-based matched cohort, including 178 cases among the exposed twins, 600 among the matched unexposed twins, and 723 among the matched singletons, corresponding to a crude incidence rate (IR) of 12.08, 7.76, and 9.33 per 1000 person-years, respectively (Table 2).

claim: 600 cases of psychiatric disorders were identified among the matched unexposed twins.
source: During the follow-up, we identified 1501 individuals with incident psychiatric disorders in the population-based matched cohort, including 178 cases among the exposed twins, 600 among the matched unexposed twins, and 723 among the matched singletons, corresponding to a crude incidence rate (IR) of 12.08, 7.76, and 9.33 per 1000 person-years, respectively (Table 2).

claim: 723 cases of psychiatric disorders were identified among the matched singletons.
source: During the follow-up, we identified 1501 individuals with incident psychiatric disorders in the population-based matched cohort, including 178 cases among the exposed twins, 600 among the matched unexposed twins, and 723 among the matched singletons, corresponding to a crude incidence rate (IR) of 12.08, 7.76, and 9.33 per 1000 person-years, respectively (Table 2).

claim: The crude incidence rate of psychiatric disorders was 12.08 per 1000 person-years among exposed twins.
source: During the follow-up, we identified 1501 individuals with incident psychiatric disorders in the population-based matched cohort, including 178 cases among the exposed twins, 600 among the matched unexposed twins, and 723 among the matched singletons, corresponding to a crude incidence rate (IR) of 12.08, 7.76, and 9.33 per 1000 person-years, respectively (Table 2).

claim: The crude incidence rate of psychiatric disorders was 7.76 per 1000 person-years among matched unexposed twins.
source: During the follow-up, we identified 1501 individuals with incident psychiatric disorders in the population-based matched cohort, including 178 cases among the exposed twins, 600 among the matched unexposed twins, and 723 among the matched singletons, corresponding to a crude incidence rate (IR) of 12.08, 7.76, and 9.33 per 1000 person-years, respectively (Table 2).

claim: The crude incidence rate of psychiatric disorders was 9.33 per 1000 person-years among matched singletons.
source: During the follow-up, we identified 1501 individuals with incident psychiatric disorders in the population-based matched cohort, including 178 cases among the exposed twins, 600 among the matched unexposed twins, and 723 among the matched singletons, corresponding to a crude incidence rate (IR) of 12.08, 7.76, and 9.33 per 1000 person-years, respectively (Table 2).

claim: The rate of any psychiatric disorders was increased among the exposed twins compared to matched unexposed twins.
source: Compared to matched unexposed twins, the rate of any psychiatric disorders was increased among the exposed twins.

claim: The hazard ratio for psychiatric disorders among exposed twins compared to unexposed twins was 1.59 (95% CI 1.33–1.90) after controlling for birth year, sex, and birth factors.
source: The hazard ratio (HR) was 1.59 (95% confidence intervals [CI] 1.33–1.90) after controlling for birth year, sex, and birth factors (i.e., GA, birth weight for GA, maternal age at birth), and decreased to 1.56 (95% CI 1.30–1.87) when other covariables, including Apgar score, family history of psychiatric disorders, and maternal educational level and cohabitation status were added into the model.
evidence: Statistical analysis result with adjustment for confounders

claim: The hazard ratio for psychiatric disorders among exposed twins compared to unexposed twins was 1.56 (95% CI 1.30–1.87) after full adjustment including Apgar score, family history of psychiatric disorders, and maternal educational level and cohabitation status.
source: The hazard ratio (HR) was 1.59 (95% confidence intervals [CI] 1.33–1.90) after controlling for birth year, sex, and birth factors (i.e., GA, birth weight for GA, maternal age at birth), and decreased to 1.56 (95% CI 1.30–1.87) when other covariables, including Apgar score, family history of psychiatric disorders, and maternal educational level and cohabitation status were added into the model.
evidence: Statistical analysis result with full adjustment

claim: The fully adjusted HR for psychiatric disorders among exposed twins compared to matched singletons was 1.41 (95% CI 1.19–1.69).
source: The fully adjusted HR was 1.41 (95% CI 1.19–1.69) when the reference group was matched singletons.
evidence: Statistical analysis result comparing to singletons

claim: In the twin-sibling family cohort, the HR for psychiatric disorders was 1.43 (95% CI 0.82–2.51) after full adjustment.
source: In the analyses of twin-sibling family cohort, we obtained an HR of 1.43 (95% CI 0.82–2.51) after full adjustment of all abovementioned variables (Table 2).
evidence: Statistical analysis result in sibling cohort

claim: Higher HRs were observed for emotional disorders compared with neurodevelopmental disorders and other psychiatric disorders, although not statistically significant.
source: Although not statistically significant, we observed higher HRs for emotional disorders such as depression and anxiety, compared with neurodevelopmental disorders and other psychiatric disorders (Table 2).

claim: The association between loss of a co-twin at birth and subsequent risk of any psychiatric disorder did not differ by sex.
source: Subgroup analyses of the population-based matched cohort indicated that the association between loss of a co-twin at birth and subsequent risk of any psychiatric disorder did not differ by sex, but seemed stronger among individuals without family history of psychiatric disorders.

claim: The association between loss of a co-twin at birth and subsequent risk of any psychiatric disorder seemed stronger among individuals without family history of psychiatric disorders.
source: Subgroup analyses of the population-based matched cohort indicated that the association between loss of a co-twin at birth and subsequent risk of any psychiatric disorder did not differ by sex, but seemed stronger among individuals without family history of psychiatric disorders.

claim: The relative risk increased further after loss of a same-sex co-twin, than loss of an opposite-sex co-twin, at birth.
source: In addition, the relative risk increased further after loss of a same-sex co-twin, than loss of an opposite-sex co-twin, at birth (Table 3).

claim: The risk elevation was only evident for psychiatric disorders diagnosed in childhood and early adulthood, that is before age of 25.
source: By plotting HRs over attained age, we found the risk elevation to be only evident for psychiatric disorders diagnosed in childhood and early adulthood, that is before age of 25 (Figure 2).
evidence: Time-varying analysis result shown in Figure 2

claim: Slightly higher HRs were obtained when comparing the exposed twins to their older siblings (1.74, 95% CI 0.54–5.59), than to their younger siblings (1.27, 95% CI 0.48–3.34).
source: We obtained slightly higher HRs when comparing the exposed twins to their older siblings (1.74, 95% CI 0.54–5.59), than to their younger siblings (1.27, 95% CI 0.48–3.34) (Supplementary file 1-Table 2).

claim: This is the first nationwide population-based and sibling-matched cohort study exploring the association between loss of a co-twin at birth or shortly after birth and the subsequent risk of psychiatric disorders.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first nationwide population-based and sibling-matched cohort study exploring the association between loss of a co-twin at birth or shortly after birth and the subsequent risk of psychiatric disorders.
evidence: Authors' statement about novelty of the study

claim: Twins exposed to a co-twin loss at birth were at considerably elevated risk of psychiatric disorders, especially emotional disorders, such as depression and anxiety, before age of 25.
source: Compared to matched unexposed twins or singletons, as well as their non-twin full siblings, twins exposed to a co-twin loss at birth were at considerably elevated risk of psychiatric disorders, especially emotional disorders, such as depression and anxiety, before age of 25.

claim: The association between co-twin loss at birth and psychiatric disorders was independent of multiple important confounders, including birth characteristics and childhood social conditions.
source: Notably, this association was independent of multiple important confounders, including birth characteristics and childhood social conditions (by comparing bereaved twins to singletons), and other familial factors (by comparing bereaved twins to their full siblings), indicating that increased clinical alertness of the mental health of surviving twins after very early co-twin loss is warranted.
evidence: Interpretation of study findings with multiple comparison groups

claim: The association between co-twin loss at birth and psychiatric disorders was independent of familial factors.
source: Notably, this association was independent of multiple important confounders, including birth characteristics and childhood social conditions (by comparing bereaved twins to singletons), and other familial factors (by comparing bereaved twins to their full siblings), indicating that increased clinical alertness of the mental health of surviving twins after very early co-twin loss is warranted.
evidence: Interpretation of study findings with sibling comparison

claim: Increased clinical alertness of the mental health of surviving twins after very early co-twin loss is warranted.
source: Notably, this association was independent of multiple important confounders, including birth characteristics and childhood social conditions (by comparing bereaved twins to singletons), and other familial factors (by comparing bereaved twins to their full siblings), indicating that increased clinical alertness of the mental health of surviving twins after very early co-twin loss is warranted.
evidence: Clinical recommendation based on study findings

claim: The excess risk of psychiatric disorders was not modified by parent's psychiatric disorder.
source: In addition, although the excess risk was not modified by parent's psychiatric disorder nor the surviving twin's congenital or other severe diseases diagnosed during follow-up, it seemed more pronounced among twins exposed to early loss of a same-sex co-twin and among twins without family history of psychiatric disorders.

claim: The excess risk of psychiatric disorders was not modified by the surviving twin's congenital or other severe diseases diagnosed during follow-up.
source: In addition, although the excess risk was not modified by parent's psychiatric disorder nor the surviving twin's congenital or other severe diseases diagnosed during follow-up, it seemed more pronounced among twins exposed to early loss of a same-sex co-twin and among twins without family history of psychiatric disorders.

claim: The excess risk of psychiatric disorders seemed more pronounced among twins exposed to early loss of a same-sex co-twin.
source: In addition, although the excess risk was not modified by parent's psychiatric disorder nor the surviving twin's congenital or other severe diseases diagnosed during follow-up, it seemed more pronounced among twins exposed to early loss of a same-sex co-twin and among twins without family history of psychiatric disorders.

claim: The excess risk of psychiatric disorders seemed more pronounced among twins without family history of psychiatric disorders.
source: In addition, although the excess risk was not modified by parent's psychiatric disorder nor the surviving twin's congenital or other severe diseases diagnosed during follow-up, it seemed more pronounced among twins exposed to early loss of a same-sex co-twin and among twins without family history of psychiatric disorders.

claim: No previous study has addressed whether emotional reactions can be observed after a very early co-twin loss where limited twin relationship, perception, or memory from the loss could be expected.
source: While accumulating evidence supports that both childhood and adult twin loss are associated with increased risk of psychiatric morbidity among the surviving twins (Rosendahl SP and Björklund, 2013; Segal and Ream, 1998), no previous study has addressed whether such emotional reactions can be observed after a very early co-twin loss where limited twin relationship, perception, or memory from the loss could be expected.

claim: The absence of evidence on very early co-twin loss is mainly due to the complexity of the research question and lack of high-quality data to address potential confounding.
source: The absence of evidence is mainly due to the complexity of the research question and lack of high-quality data to address potential confounding by multiple factors, such as twin pregnancy and birth (i.e., suboptimal birth characteristics) but a singleton-like life, familial factors, and genetic susceptibility to diseases.

claim: The higher relative risk observed after early loss of a same-sex co-twin, compared with a loss of opposite-sex co-twin, may indicate the importance of shared genetic background on the formation of a twinship bond.
source: Particularly, despite the lack of information on zygosity, the higher relative risk observed after early loss of a same-sex co-twin, compared with a loss of opposite-sex co-twin, may indicate the importance of shared genetic background on the formation of a twinship bond.
evidence: Interpretation of findings with speculative language 'may indicate'

claim: Greater grief intensity has been reported among monozygotic twins who experienced an adult loss of co-twin, compared with dizygotic twins.
source: This is similar to the greater grief intensity reported among monozygotic twins who experienced an adult loss of co-twin, compared with dizygotic twins, and consistent with the evolutionary theory suggesting a role of genetic relatedness in the bereavement process (Segal and Blozis, 2002; Segal, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Segal and Blozis, 2002; Segal, 2019

claim: Evolutionary theory suggests a role of genetic relatedness in the bereavement process.
source: This is similar to the greater grief intensity reported among monozygotic twins who experienced an adult loss of co-twin, compared with dizygotic twins, and consistent with the evolutionary theory suggesting a role of genetic relatedness in the bereavement process (Segal and Blozis, 2002; Segal, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Segal and Blozis, 2002; Segal, 2019

claim: The death of a co-twin at birth may be an indicator of a poor pregnancy or birth conditions or congenital defects that are shared within a twin pair.
source: The major concern in studies of this kind is that, the death of a co-twin at birth may be an indicator of a poor pregnancy or birth conditions or congenital defects that are shared within a twin pair, and hence vulnerability of the surviving twin to various diseases (such as developmental defects and other somatic disorders) during their later lives.
evidence: Discussion of potential confounding with speculative language 'may be'

claim: Similar results were obtained in sensitivity analyses where the presence of congenital abnormalities and the diagnosis of severe somatic conditions during follow-up were taken into account.
source: However, similar results were obtained in our sensitivity analyses where the presence of congenital abnormalities and the diagnosis of severe somatic conditions during follow-up were taken into account by subgroup analyses or by additional adjustments, suggesting a minor influence of these factors.

claim: The sensitivity analyses suggest a minor influence of congenital abnormalities and severe somatic conditions on the observed association.
source: However, similar results were obtained in our sensitivity analyses where the presence of congenital abnormalities and the diagnosis of severe somatic conditions during follow-up were taken into account by subgroup analyses or by additional adjustments, suggesting a minor influence of these factors.

claim: Altered parenting of the grieving parents could be a possible explanation for the observed increased risk of psychiatric disorders among the surviving twins.
source: Another possible explanation for the observed increased risk of psychiatric disorders among the surviving twins could be altered parenting of the grieving parents.

claim: A heightened risk of psychiatric disorder was observed in full siblings, especially younger full siblings, of the bereaved twins.
source: Indeed, given that we also observed a heightened risk of psychiatric disorder in full siblings, especially younger full siblings, of the bereaved twins in our twin-sibling family analysis, altered parenting style among bereaved individuals and its impact on offspring's mental health need further investigation.

claim: Altered parenting style among bereaved individuals and its impact on offspring's mental health need further investigation.
source: Indeed, given that we also observed a heightened risk of psychiatric disorder in full siblings, especially younger full siblings, of the bereaved twins in our twin-sibling family analysis, altered parenting style among bereaved individuals and its impact on offspring's mental health need further investigation.

claim: Additional analyses suggest limited mediating role of clinically confirmed parental psychiatric disorders in the association between early co-twin loss and risk of psychiatric disorder.
source: Our additional analyses taking into account clinically confirmed psychiatric disorders of the bereaved parents during the follow-up suggest limited mediating role of clinically confirmed parental psychiatric disorders in the association between early co-twin loss and risk of psychiatric disorder.

claim: Severe mental illness requiring a clinical diagnosis affects a relatively small proportion of the bereaved parents.
source: Nevertheless, severe mental illness requiring a clinical diagnosis affects a relatively small proportion of the bereaved parents.
evidence: Contextual information about parental psychiatric disorders

claim: The study used a population-based cohort design, including 787 exposed twins with a complete follow-up of up to 41 years.
source: The major merit of our study is the use of population-based cohort design, including 787 exposed twins with a complete follow-up of up to 41 years.

claim: The possible influence of twin pregnancy and twin birth was controlled through the twin-twin comparison.
source: In addition to a full consideration of birth factors, the possible influence of twin pregnancy and twin birth was controlled through the twin-twin comparison, while the social conditions during childhood was taken into consideration in the twin-singleton comparison.

claim: The social conditions during childhood was taken into consideration in the twin-singleton comparison.
source: In addition to a full consideration of birth factors, the possible influence of twin pregnancy and twin birth was controlled through the twin-twin comparison, while the social conditions during childhood was taken into consideration in the twin-singleton comparison.

claim: Through the twin-full sibling comparison, the study was able to control for potential familial confounders.
source: Through the twin-full sibling comparison, we were further able to control for potential familial confounders, as well as explore possible underlying mechanisms related to parenting.

claim: Through the twin-full sibling comparison, the study was able to explore possible underlying mechanisms related to parenting.
source: Through the twin-full sibling comparison, we were further able to control for potential familial confounders, as well as explore possible underlying mechanisms related to parenting.

claim: The study had sufficient statistical power to perform most of the planned subgroup analyses.
source: As the largest cohort study on co-twin loss at birth to date, we had sufficient statistical power to perform most of the planned subgroup analyses.

claim: Information bias was minimized since the registration and diagnosis of exposure and outcome was compiled prospectively and independently.
source: Information bias was minimized since the registration and diagnosis of exposure and outcome was compiled prospectively and independently.
evidence: Study design feature to minimize bias

source: Limitations include the late establishment of outpatient care records in the Swedish National Patient Register (2001-), which may have rendered an underestimated number of psychiatric disorder diagnoses, especially the milder ones.
evidence: Study limitation with speculative language 'may have'

claim: Individuals were relatively young at the end of follow-up (up to 41 years, with median age at follow-up as 19 years).
source: In addition, individuals were relatively young at the end of follow-up (up to 41 years, with median age at follow-up as 19 years).

claim: The study focused mainly on early-onset psychiatric disorders.
source: Therefore, the study focused mainly on early-onset psychiatric disorders.

claim: The association between loss of a co-twin at birth and psychiatric disorders beyond early adulthood needs to be addressed in further studies.
source: The association between loss of a co-twin at birth and psychiatric disorders beyond early adulthood needs to be addressed in further studies.

claim: The study involved merely twins who lost their co-twin at or shortly after delivery.
source: Furthermore, because we identified individuals through the unique personal identification numbers assigned at birth to each Swedish-born person, our study involved merely twins who lost their co-twin at or shortly after delivery.

claim: The loss of a co-twin during the early pregnancy period (i.e., vanishing twin) or due to stillbirth is beyond the scope of the present study.
source: The loss of a co-twin during the early pregnancy period (i.e., vanishing twin) or due to stillbirth, which might also have psychological effects on the surviving twin (A Silent Cry, 2008), is therefore beyond the scope of the present study.

claim: The loss of a co-twin during the early pregnancy period or due to stillbirth might have psychological effects on the surviving twin.
source: The loss of a co-twin during the early pregnancy period (i.e., vanishing twin) or due to stillbirth, which might also have psychological effects on the surviving twin (A Silent Cry, 2008), is therefore beyond the scope of the present study.
evidence: Supported by citation with speculative language 'might have'

claim: The possibility of residual confounding cannot be excluded.
source: Finally, although we made every effort to control for important confounders such as birth characteristics, social and familial conditions, and shared genetic background, we cannot exclude the possibility of residual confounding.

claim: In the Swedish population, exposure to death of a co-twin at birth was associated with a subsequently elevated risk of psychiatric disorders among the surviving twin.
source: In conclusion, in the Swedish population, exposure to death of a co-twin at birth was associated with a subsequently elevated risk of psychiatric disorders among the surviving twin.

claim: These findings call for medical and scientific attention of the mental health of this bereaved population.
source: These findings call for medical and scientific attention of the mental health of this bereaved population and further exploration of the underlying mechanisms.

claim: Further exploration of the underlying mechanisms linking co-twin loss at birth to psychiatric disorders is needed.
source: These findings call for medical and scientific attention of the mental health of this bereaved population and further exploration of the underlying mechanisms.

claim: All individuals born in Sweden between 1973 and 2011 were identified based on the Swedish Total Population Register.
source: Based on the Swedish Total Population Register, we identified all individuals born in Sweden between 1973 and 2011.

claim: Twin pairs were identified as having the same biological father and mother and born on the same day (+/- 1 day), excluding multiple births.
source: Utilizing the personal identification numbers that are uniquely assigned to all Swedish residents, we linked the data to the Multi-Generation Register and identified all twin pairs (i.e., having the same biological father and mother and born on the same day (+/- 1 day), excluding multiple births) and singletons (i.e., the only baby during a single delivery).

claim: Singletons were identified as the only baby during a single delivery.
source: Utilizing the personal identification numbers that are uniquely assigned to all Swedish residents, we linked the data to the Multi-Generation Register and identified all twin pairs (i.e., having the same biological father and mother and born on the same day (+/- 1 day), excluding multiple births) and singletons (i.e., the only baby during a single delivery).

claim: All included individuals had to have survived at least 60 days after birth and have available information in MBR.
source: In order to enter the study, all included individuals had to have survived at least 60 days after birth and have available information in MBR, which has collected nationwide information on deliveries in Sweden since 1973.

claim: The Medical Birth Register has collected nationwide information on deliveries in Sweden since 1973.
source: In order to enter the study, all included individuals had to have survived at least 60 days after birth and have available information in MBR, which has collected nationwide information on deliveries in Sweden since 1973.

claim: Twins have considerably elevated mortality rate during the first and second months after birth.
source: Because twins have considerably elevated mortality rate during the first and second months after birth and to maximize the sample size of the exposed twins in our study, we defined loss of a co-twin at birth as a death of the co-twin within 60 days after birth, according to information obtained from the Causes of Death Register, which is available electronically for register-based research since 1952.
evidence: Rationale for study definition based on established knowledge

claim: Loss of a co-twin at birth was defined as a death of the co-twin within 60 days after birth.
source: Because twins have considerably elevated mortality rate during the first and second months after birth and to maximize the sample size of the exposed twins in our study, we defined loss of a co-twin at birth as a death of the co-twin within 60 days after birth, according to information obtained from the Causes of Death Register, which is available electronically for register-based research since 1952.

claim: The Causes of Death Register is available electronically for register-based research since 1952.
source: Because twins have considerably elevated mortality rate during the first and second months after birth and to maximize the sample size of the exposed twins in our study, we defined loss of a co-twin at birth as a death of the co-twin within 60 days after birth, according to information obtained from the Causes of Death Register, which is available electronically for register-based research since 1952.

claim: Among 88,636 eligible twins, 787 had a co-twin that died at birth or within 60th days after birth.
source: As shown in Figure 1, among 88,636 eligible twins, 787 had a co-twin that died at birth or within 60th days after birth and were included in the exposed group.
evidence: Study population data shown in Figure 1

claim: The 60th day after birth was considered as the date of cohort entry (index date) for exposed twins.
source: The 60th day after birth was considered as the date of cohort entry (index date) for exposed twins.

claim: Five unexposed twins per exposed twin were randomly selected from the twin population on the index date of the exposed twin.
source: First, with the aim of controlling for twin pregnancy and twin birth, five unexposed twins (with a co-twin that survived at least 60 days after birth) per exposed twin were randomly selected from the twin population on the index date of the exposed twin (i.e., also the index date for unexposed twins).
evidence: Study design for first reference group

claim: Unexposed twins were individually matched to the exposed twin by birth year, sex, and GA.
source: They were individually matched to the exposed twin by birth year, sex, and GA (<28, 28–31, 32–36, or ≥37 weeks).

claim: Five singletons per exposed twin were selected from the singleton population on the index date of the exposed twin.
source: Second, as the exposed twins grew up on their own, as singletons, in order to control for such social conditions, five singletons per exposed twin were also selected from the singleton population, on the index date of the exposed twin (i.e., also the index date for matched singletons).
evidence: Study design for second reference group

claim: Matched singletons were individually matched to the exposed twins on sex, birth year, GA, birth weight for GA, and birth order.
source: Because we had a larger pool for selection of matched singletons, compared with selection of unexposed twins, we were able to use more matching variables, including sex, birth year, GA (<28, 28–31, 32–36, or ≥37 weeks), birth weight for GA (<10th, 10–30th, 31–50th, 51–70th, 71–90th, or >90th percentile), and birth order (1st, 2nd, 3rd, ≥4th child within a family), to ensure the comparability between twins and singletons with regard to birth characteristics.

claim: Non-twin full siblings of the exposed twins were included on the index date of the exposed twins or 60 days after their own birth, if born later than the twins.
source: To address the concern about familial confounders, such as genetic background and environmental factors during childhood shared within a family, we further constructed a twin-sibling family cohort where non-twin full siblings of the exposed twins, if any, identified through the Multi-Generation Register, were included on the index date of the exposed twins or 60 days after their own birth, if born later than the twins (i.e., the index date for non-twin full siblings).

claim: Follow-up lasted until the occurrence of any or a specific type of psychiatric disorders, death, emigration, or the end of follow-up (December 31, 2013), whichever occurred first.
source: Follow-up of all study participants started from the index date and lasted until the occurrence of any or a specific type of psychiatric disorders, death, emigration, or the end of follow-up (December 31, 2013), whichever occurred first.

claim: Any first-ever inpatient or outpatient hospital visit with a psychiatric disorder as one of the registered diagnoses during the follow-up was identified from the NPR.
source: Any first-ever inpatient or outpatient hospital visit with a psychiatric disorder as one of the registered diagnoses, primary or secondary, during the follow-up was identified from the NPR (ICD eight and ICD nine codes: 290–315, ICD 10 codes: F00-F99).

claim: Psychiatric disorders were identified using ICD eight and ICD nine codes: 290–315, and ICD 10 codes: F00-F99.
source: Any first-ever inpatient or outpatient hospital visit with a psychiatric disorder as one of the registered diagnoses, primary or secondary, during the follow-up was identified from the NPR (ICD eight and ICD nine codes: 290–315, ICD 10 codes: F00-F99).
evidence: Diagnostic codes used for outcome identification

claim: Birth weight z-score was generated for GA, sex, and twin/singleton-specific populations to calculate birth weight for gestational age percentiles.
source: Specifically, to calculate the birth weight for gestational age percentiles, we generated birth weight z-score for GA, sex, and twin/singleton-specific populations and categorized it into <10th, 10–30th, 31–50th, 51–70th, 71–90th, and >90th percentile.

claim: A poor neonatal condition was defined as the presence of low Apgar score (≤7) at 5 or 10 min after birth.
source: We considered a poor neonatal condition as the presence of low Apgar score (≤7) at 5 or 10 min after birth.

claim: Family history of psychiatric disorders was defined as any diagnosis of or death due to psychiatric disorder or suicide among the first-degree relatives of the study participants.
source: Family history of psychiatric disorders was defined as any diagnosis of or death due to psychiatric disorder or suicide among the first-degree relatives (i.e., biological parents and siblings) of the study participants, according to the NPR or Causes of Death Register.

claim: The study was approved by the Regional Ethics Review Board in Stockholm, Sweden.
source: The study was approved by the Regional Ethics Review Board in Stockholm, Sweden.

claim: The association between loss of a co-twin at birth and risk of psychiatric disorders was estimated using HRs with 95% CIs, derived from conditional Cox regression models where the attained age was applied as the underlying time scale.
source: We estimated the association between loss of a co-twin at birth and risk of psychiatric disorders using HRs with 95% CIs, derived from conditional Cox regression models where the attained age was applied as the underlying time scale.

claim: No significant effect modification was found by the presence of psychiatric disorders among parents.
source: In sensitivity analyses, we found no significant effect modification by the presence of psychiatric disorders among parents (Supplementary file 1-Table 2), by the presence of congenital abnormalities, or by the diagnoses of severe somatic diseases during follow-up (Supplementary file 1-Table 3).

claim: No significant effect modification was found by the presence of congenital abnormalities.
source: In sensitivity analyses, we found no significant effect modification by the presence of psychiatric disorders among parents (Supplementary file 1-Table 2), by the presence of congenital abnormalities, or by the diagnoses of severe somatic diseases during follow-up (Supplementary file 1-Table 3).

claim: No significant effect modification was found by the diagnoses of severe somatic diseases during follow-up.
source: In sensitivity analyses, we found no significant effect modification by the presence of psychiatric disorders among parents (Supplementary file 1-Table 2), by the presence of congenital abnormalities, or by the diagnoses of severe somatic diseases during follow-up (Supplementary file 1-Table 3).

claim: Changing the definition of loss of a co-twin at birth to loss of a co-twin within 28 days after birth yielded largely similar estimates, although with lower precision.
source: Moreover, changing the definition of loss of a co-twin at birth to loss of a co-twin within 28 days after birth yielded largely similar estimates, although with lower precision (Supplementary file 1-Table 4).

claim: The HR for neurodevelopmental disorders among exposed twins compared to unexposed twins was 1.56 (95% CI 1.16–2.08).
The HR for emotional disorders among exposed twins compared to unexposed twins was 1.90 (95% CI 1.49–2.42).
The HR for other psychiatric disorders among exposed twins compared to unexposed twins was 1.32 (95% CI 1.02–1.70).
The HR for psychiatric disorders among male exposed twins compared to unexposed twins was 1.74 (95% CI 1.37–2.22).
The HR for psychiatric disorders among female exposed twins compared to unexposed twins was 1.37 (95% CI 1.04–1.81).
The HR for psychiatric disorders among exposed twins without family history compared to unexposed twins was 1.62 (95% CI 1.33–1.97).
The HR for psychiatric disorders among exposed twins who lost a same-sex co-twin compared to unexposed twins was 1.69 (95% CI 1.34–2.12).
The HR for psychiatric disorders among exposed twins who lost an opposite-sex co-twin compared to unexposed twins was 1.30 (95% CI 0.81–2.10).
Figure 2 shows time-varying hazard ratios for psychiatric disorders over attained age.
source: By plotting HRs over attained age, we found the risk elevation to be only evident for psychiatric disorders diagnosed in childhood and early adulthood, that is before age of 25 (Figure 2).
evidence: Reference to Figure 2 showing time-varying analysis

claim: Time-varying hazard ratios were derived from flexible parametric survival models, allowing relative risk of psychiatric disorders to vary over attained age.
source: Time-varying hazard ratios were derived from flexible parametric survival models, allowing relative risk of psychiatric disorders to vary over attained age.

claim: A spline with five df (four intermediate knots and two knots at each boundary, placed at quintiles of distribution of events) was used for the baseline rate in the flexible parametric models.
source: A spline with five df (four intermediate knots and two knots at each boundary, placed at quintiles of distribution of events) was used for the baseline rate, while three df was used for the time-varying effect.

claim: Three df was used for the time-varying effect in the flexible parametric models.
source: A spline with five df (four intermediate knots and two knots at each boundary, placed at quintiles of distribution of events) was used for the baseline rate, while three df was used for the time-varying effect.
